title: A Dark Bedroom May Be Better for Your Heart
paragraphs: Experts have long advised people to keep their bedrooms dark in order to sleep well. Now, a major new study suggests that sleeping in a dark room may also be important for protecting the heart.

The study, which was published in the European Heart Journal in September 2026, used data from the UK Biobank, a large database containing health information on hundreds of thousands of people in the UK. One part of the study involved more than 10,000 adults who did not have heart disease. For one week, they wore devices on their wrists that measured the amount of light around them. About three years later, they had scans of their hearts.

The researchers found that people who were exposed to more light at night tended to have larger heart chambers and thicker heart walls, and their hearts pumped slightly less efficiently. The more light people were exposed to, the greater these changes were. In the group with the most exposure, people spent an average of almost 34 minutes a night in light brighter than 3 lux, which is roughly equal to the light of three candles placed about a meter from the bed. Although these changes did not cause any obvious symptoms, the researchers believe they are medically important.

In another part of the study, the researchers followed about 70,000 adults for eight to ten years. Compared with people who had no light exposure at night, those with the most exposure had a 29% higher risk of heart failure, a 24% higher risk of heart attack and a 33% higher risk of stroke. The researchers found that shorter sleep partly explained the link. Light at night is known to reduce the body's production of melatonin, a hormone that helps control sleep.

According to Lu Qi, an epidemiologist at Tulane University, light pollution has emerged as a new risk factor for heart disease. However, because the study was observational, it cannot prove that light at night directly causes heart problems.
To keep bedrooms dark, experts recommend using blackout curtains, turning off lights on electronic devices and wearing a sleep mask.
